transcript:
[00:00] Tom (Redwood AE): All right everyone, welcome, thanks for joining. We're about 55 minutes today, rough agenda: quick convo about your goals, then Aisha will walk the Optimize console quant profiles, then open Q&A and next steps.

[00:18] Raj (Nimbus CTO): Thanks Tom. Couple of things up front — our main ask is to cut token bill by at least 40% for the summarization pipeline without losing clinical details. We have a 95th pctl latency target around 450ms end-to-end.

[00:37] Tom: Got it, 40% cost drop is a good target to aim for. Aisha, want to jump in?

[00:42] Aisha (Redwood SE): Yeah, sure. Quick caveat, I'll say Red wood Optimize — or Redwood Optmize, apologies, I always say it too fast — this is the console area that suggests quant profiles, runs sensitivity sweeps, and generates heatmaps of perf vs fidelity. I'll share my screen now.

[01:05] Speaker 1 (screen share noise): uh screen sharing — can everyone see my browser?

[01:10] Mei (Lead ML Eng): We can see it yes. Font's a bit small.

[01:15] Aisha: Cool. So first panel: workload characterization. We ingest your prompt samples and runtime traces, then we estimate token distributions, prefix reuse, KV cache hit rate — sometimes the autosampler mislabels KV as K V cache in the reports, ignore the spacing there.

[01:34] Oliver (SRE): Quick question: we do heavy prefix reuse for patient history snippets — will that push you toward INT8 or FP8?

[01:41] Aisha: Great question. Prefix reuse favors batching + KV caching which tends to benefit INT8 more because of smaller memory pressure and faster memory copies. But that's not the whole story — for certain decoder layers FP8 gives better numerical fidelity for edge cases, e.g., hallucination around numeric sequences.

[02:02] Mei: When you say hallucination, do you have metrics? Like ROUGE or a clinical QA metric?

[02:07] Aisha: We run pairwise comparisons against your golden set — we can ingest your clinical QA tests. For the demo I have a synthetic example showing answer correctness and a 'clinical fidelity' pass rate.

[02:20] Tom: I'll add here that you can plug in any eval set into the Optimize console; it will run the models at different precisions and return quality deltas aligned with your metric.

[02:33] [02:33] Aisha: Switching to the quant sweeper. This widget runs INT8-only sweeps, FP8-only sweeps, and mixed-precision knobs. See this heatmap — x-axis is latency, y-axis is relative quality delta, colors are cost per 1k tokens. The green band is our recommended pareto front.

[02:56] Raj: That heatmap looks familiar — how is latency measured? Is it CPU-to-GPU or end-to-end from API?

[03:03] Aisha: Good catch. By default it's server-side token latency measured at the serving runtime. We also can instrument end-to-end in the sandbox to incorporate network and client-side overheads. For your numbers we should enable end-to-end traces.

[03:20] Mei: Can you highlight an example where INT8 was actually worse in quality?

[03:26] Aisha: Sure — here's an INT8 profile that drops latency 35% but causes a 6% drop in our clinical QA pass rate on long-context numeric extraction tasks. FP8 at that same latency only drops 1.5%. So the console will surface those different deltas.

[03:46] [03:46] Tom: Also note we have profile-level rollouts: you can do a canary where 5% of traffic uses FP8, 95% uses baseline, and monitor automatic regression alerts.

[03:57] Sofia (Product): How do rollbacks happen if we see regression?

[04:01] Aisha: Automatic fallback — the routing layer swaps to the last known-good model/profile and you get a notification. There's also real-time trace search to pull examples that failed the QA checks.

[04:17] Oliver: About the memory/cost math — what's the billed unit? Do we pay per vCPU? GPU time?

[04:24] Tom: Hosted API is usage-based per token plus model-specific multiplier. Dedicated has reserved capacity pricing. For the pilot we'll model cost on your 30-day traffic trace; Optimize will output estimated monthly spend for each profile.

[04:39] [04:39] Mei: Can we run the bench against a private deployment? Some of our data can't leave our VPC.

[04:45] Aisha: Yes — Optimize supports private and dedicated. For private we deploy a local probe that runs the same sweeps against your cluster. The only data that leaves is aggregate stats unless you opt in to share samples.

[04:59] Raj: Ok good. Steps: we need a non-prod env first. What's required?

[05:05] Aisha: Minimal: a node with GPU runtime compatible with our inference engine (we'll provide an installer), and network access to the control plane for reporting. If you want air-gapped, there's an on-prem bundle but that adds some ops overhead.

[05:20] [05:20] Aisha: Back to the console — here's a tab called "Sensitivity sweep details". This iterates quant configurations, runs the eval set, and spits out token-level diffs. Note the transcription here sometimes reads FP8 as F P eight in the UI export, so when you get the export don't be alarmed.

[05:41] Mei: What's the compute delta typically, like vram usage?

[05:45] Aisha: Typically INT8 reduces peak VRAM by ~30-40% depending on model and sequence length; FP8 sits between INT8 and FP16 depending on kernel support. That reduction often translates directly to higher concurrency and lower p95 latency under load.

[06:01] [06:01] Tom: We run a small live bench now — Aisha can show a canned workload that mirrors your 512-token summarization.

[06:08] Aisha: Running the canned bench... initializing. You'll see two runs: baseline FP16, then INT8 and FP8 variants.

[06:18] [06:18] (Demo noise: bench running)

[06:35] Aisha: First results coming in. Baseline p95 token latency 12ms per token, end-to-end ~410ms for 512 tokens in this env. INT8 optimized run shows 8ms per token, end-to-end ~300ms. FP8 is 9.5ms per token, end-to-end ~340ms, with smaller quality delta.

[06:58] Raj: Those numbers look promising. How reproducible are they on A100 vs H100 vs third-party clouds?

[07:06] Aisha: We have performance profiles per hardware in the catalog. H100 shows best FP8 throughput due to tensor core support; A100 often favors INT8 on some kernels. We include kernel selection notes in the profile export.

[07:25] Mei: Are there any gotchas with mixed-precision on custom ops? We use a custom tokeniser and a small post-processing step.

[07:32] Aisha: Custom ops can break quantization assumptions if they alter ranges. We recommend running a small calibration pass; Optimize can auto-generate calibration data and validate downstream post-processing with your unit tests.

[07:48] [07:48] Oliver: How about caching — if we have a heavy KV cache hit rate, does that change per-token latency significantly?

[07:55] Aisha: KV cache improves latency for repeated prefixes; however if your cache hit rate is high, INT8's memory savings let you keep larger cache resident which further reduces end-to-end. The console includes a simulated cache-hit heatmap.

[08:11] Tom: Quick interruption — Mei, you mentioned clinical fidelity. Can you describe a couple of concrete failure modes we should watch for?

[08:19] Mei: Sure — number extraction from discharge notes, and sometimes hallucinated medication names in summaries. If we lose those, product and compliance teams will flag it.

[08:28] Aisha: We'll prioritize those checks in the eval set. The Optimize console can mark tests as "blocking" — any regression on those blocks the profile rollouts.

[08:41] [08:41] (crosstalk) Sofia: Is there an audit log of who kicked off a rollout? We need traceability.

[08:46] Tom: Yes, audit logs with SAML-based SSO mapping to emails, and a change history in the console.

[08:55] Raj: Security question — KMS/HSM integration? We need to ensure keys never leave our vault.

[09:02] Aisha: For private deployments we integrate with customer KMS. For hosted, we offer envelope encryption with customer-managed keys. We can include an architecture whitepaper after the call.

[09:15] [09:15] Aisha: Back to the bench — I'm going to toggle mixed-precision where embedding layers are FP16 and transformer weights INT8. This often gives a decent compromise.

[09:28] (bench running)

[09:44] Aisha: Mixed-precision results are in: latency similar to INT8 but quality closer to FP8, cost about 22% lower than baseline in this run.

[09:58] Mei: How do you recommend we roll this out? Full cutover or staged?

[10:03] Aisha: Staged. Canary -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with automated rollback triggers based on your QA set and real-time production signals. We can wire alerts to PagerDuty.

[10:14] [10:14] Tom: I also want to call out the Optimize suggestions engine — it will propose quantization schemas but also suggest sequence-length bucketing to avoid worst-case latency when you occasionally hit 2k tokens.

[10:28] Raj: Bucketting means we route long-tail requests to a higher-precision lane?

[10:33] Aisha: Exactly — policy-based routing: short queries to INT8 lane, long queries to FP8/FP16 lane. That keeps p95 in check.

[10:45] Oliver: Does that add complexity to our API clients?

[10:48] Tom: No, routing is transparent at the platform layer; you can annotate requests with hints but not required.

[10:55] [10:55] Mei: You mentioned earlier automatic calibration — what about offline calibration for very sensitive models?

[11:01] Aisha: We provide an offline calibration tool that runs on your data in your VPC, generates quantization tables, and signs them. Those tables can be imported into the runtime.

[11:14] Sofia: For compliance, can we get a report of which examples failed and why?

[11:19] Aisha: Yes — the console produces differential example reports with token diffs and a human-readable note like "truncated numeric token" or "low-confidence replacement". Sometimes the auto-note is noisy but it's a good starting point.

[11:33] [11:33] (pause)

[11:40] Tom: Let's surface a concrete pilot plan. I'm proposing: 2-week data intake + sandbox setup, 72-hour continuous quant bench running INT8/FP8/mixed profiles, then a 2-week canary with blocking checks. Budget estimate to follow. Everyone okay with that?

[11:58] Raj: Sounds fine. Timing wise we want end-to-end in mid-May if possible.

[12:05] Aisha: We can align to that.

[12:10] [12:10] (Customer asks quick clarifying question)

[12:18] Mei: One more technical: how do you handle softmax stability in INT8? We've seen NaNs in older quant libs.

[12:24] Aisha: Our runtime uses scaled-softmax with range-clipping and per-layer dynamic scaling to avoid NaNs; we also have nightly regression tests on a broad model corpus.

[12:36] Oliver: Are there specific architectures where FP8 is a no-brainer? Like very deep LLMs or mixture-of-experts?

[12:43] Aisha: MoE and very deep transformers sometimes prefer FP8 for critical layers due to accumulator range. We call out those recommendations in each model's profile.

[12:55] [12:55] (Demo: exporting report)

[13:05] Aisha: Exporting the sweep report — it generates CSVs, a heatmap PNG, and a JSON with recommended rollout percentages. I'll email the artifact after the call.

[13:14] Tom: Quick note—sometimes the JSON keys are slightly different between on-prem and hosted exports; we'll normalize before sending. Sorry for that little inconsistency.

[13:25] Raj: No problem. A few governance questions: who from Redwood will be our day-to-day contact during pilot?

[13:31] Tom: I'll be the AE owner, Aisha will run the technical bench, and Lena will coordinate enablement and onboarding.

[13:40] Mei: For the bench, can you also output per-class precision/recall for our named-entity types?

[13:46] Aisha: Yes — send the entity list and we will add class-level stats into the sensitivity report.

[13:55] [13:55] (small technical digression — network peering)

[14:12] Oliver: About peering — can we do VPC peering or private link for the probe?

[14:16] Tom: We support both; peering is simplest. We'll share network requirements in the checklist.

[14:25] Sofia: I have a product question — would you recommend pinning a model version or letting Redwood auto-roll?

[14:31] Aisha: Pinning is safest for clinical workflows. You can still use Optimize to recommend profiles for that pinned version. Auto-roll is better for more exploratory apps.

[14:43] [14:43] Mei: Any mention of model distillation in this flow? Could we further compress?

[14:48] Aisha: Optimize focuses on serving-time quant/profile tuning. Distillation is a complementary upstream approach — we can partner with our model team for a separate engagement.

[15:00] Raj: OK last set of questions: SLA, error budgets, and how you measure them in trials.

[15:05] Tom: Dedicated customers get SLA-backed latency SLOs. For pilot we'll agree on an error budget and run benchmarks under a stress load to define expected p95. We'll include those numbers in the pilot doc.

[15:19] [15:19] Aisha: I'm going to quickly demo the drift detection feature — it flags distribution shifts in prompts and can re-trigger sensitivity sweeps automatically.

[15:29] Mei: Does it run continuously in production?

[15:32] Aisha: Yes, lightweight monitors run in the control plane and push alerts when thresholds cross.

[15:38] (15:38) Tom: We're at about 40 minutes in. Any final blockers?

[15:42] Raj: None from me; want to see the bench results on our data before committing.

[15:46] Mei: Same. Also need cost breakdown per 100k requests.

[15:50] Tom: We'll include per-100k estimates in the cost model we send.

[15:55] [15:55] (closing remarks)

[16:00] Tom: Great — recap of next steps: Tom to send sandbox access and pricing, Mei to upload eval set and SLOs, Aisha to run bench and share heatmap. We'll schedule follow-up for Apr 20th. Any objections?

[16:15] Raj: No objections. Thanks everyone.

[16:20] Sofia: Thanks, bye.

[16:24] (meeting ends)
